summary: Defines a Management Information Base for Proxy Mobile IPv6. It lets network management systems monitor and control the mobile access gateway and the local mobility anchor.

eli5.summary: A MIB is a list of gauges and switches for a device. This one is for the equipment that keeps a roaming phone connected, so a manager can check on it and tweak it.

questions: how to monitor pmipv6 with snmp
what is a mobile access gateway
what is a local mobility anchor
subtitle: SNMP objects for watching and tuning the gateways and anchors that keep a roaming device connected under Proxy Mobile IPv6.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 moves a device between access links without the device taking part in the signaling, but operators had no standard way to monitor or control the network entities that do the work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two SNMP MIB modules, PMIPV6-TC-MIB and PMIPV6-MIB, with objects for the mobile access gateway (MAG) and the local mobility anchor (LMA): capabilities, binding tables, configuration, counters and notifications.
tldr.outcome: A management system can read binding state, see why registrations were rejected, change a few timers and receive tunnel up and down notifications. Write access needs SNMPv3 protection.

today: RFC 6475 is a Proposed Standard from May 2012. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it extends the Mobile IPv6 MIB in RFC 4295 for the protocol defined in RFC 5213.

sections.title: The Management Framework
sections.content: RFC 6475 defines a portion of the Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) Management Information Base, or MIB. Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, normally by the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects are defined with the Structure of Management Information, and this memo uses SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580). The overall framework is described in RFC 3410.
sections.eli5: A MIB is like a big list of readings and settings that a manager program can ask a device about, using a standard language.

sections.title: PMIPv6 Entities and What Needs Managing
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213) extends Mobile IPv6 to give network-based localized mobility management to IPv6 nodes in a PMIPv6 domain. The RFC names three entities. The mobile node (MN) is an IP host or router whose mobility the network manages. The local mobility anchor (LMA) is the home agent for the mobile node and the topological anchor point for its home network prefixes, and it manages the binding state. The mobile access gateway (MAG) sits on an access router, tracks the mobile node's movements and signals the LMA.

The requirements section lists four things to monitor: the capabilities of PMIPv6 entities, signaling traffic, binding-related details at the LMA and MAG, and binding-related statistics.
sections.eli5: When your phone moves between Wi-Fi spots, a helper at each spot and a main helper behind them do the paperwork. This MIB lets a manager look at how both helpers are doing.

sections.title: MIB Design and Object Groups
sections.content:
The design principle is to keep the MIB as simple as possible while meeting the essential needs of monitoring and control. PMIPV6-MIB extends the Mobile IPv6 MIB (MIPV6-MIB, RFC 4295) and is assumed to always be implemented together with it. It uses textual conventions from the INET-ADDRESS-MIB and the IP-MIB.

The objects fall into groups: pmip6Core for objects common to all PMIPv6 entities (including the binding cache table), pmip6Mag for the MAG, pmip6Lma for the LMA and pmip6Notifications for asynchronous events. The MAG side has tables for proxy care-of addresses, mobile node identifiers, link-layer identifiers, home network prefixes, the binding update list and mobile node policy profiles. The LMA side has tables for LMA addresses, identifiers and home network prefixes.

IANA assigned base arcs in the mib-2 tree for both modules.
sections.eli5: The control panel is split into a part for the main helper, a part for the local helpers, a shared part, and a part that rings a bell when something happens.

sections.title: The Textual Conventions Module
sections.content:
PMIPV6-TC-MIB defines reusable data types so that other PMIPv6-related MIB modules need not invent their own. It includes a 64-bit timestamp (Pmip6TimeStamp64) where the first 48 bits hold whole seconds since January 1, 1970 and the remaining 16 bits hold 1/65536 fractions of a second. It also defines the mobile node identifier and link-layer identifier (octet strings of 0 to 255 bytes), and two index types, Pmip6MnIndex and Pmip6MnLLIndex, which are management-assigned integers from 1 to 4294967295.

Pmip6MnInterfaceATT names the access technology that connects the mobile node to the MAG, as a value from 0 to 12.
sections.eli5: This part defines the kinds of labels used on the panel, like a clock format, an ID tag and a number for each roaming device.

sections.title: Capabilities and Tunable Settings
sections.content:
The object pmip6Capabilities is a read-only bit field: mobilityAccessGateway(0) and localMobilityAnchor(1). One entity may support both functions.

Some objects are read-write. On the LMA, pmip6LmaMinDelayBeforeBCEDelete is the time to wait before deleting a binding cache entry after a Proxy Binding Update with lifetime 0 (default 10000 milliseconds). pmip6LmaMaxDelayBeforeNewBCEAssign is how long to wait for a de-registration before creating a new mobility session (default 1500 milliseconds). pmip6LmaTimestampValidityWindow is the largest allowed difference between a message timestamp and the LMA's clock (default 300 milliseconds). The flag pmip6MobileNodeGeneratedTimestampInUse defaults to false.
sections.eli5: Some knobs on the panel set how long a helper waits before forgetting a device, and how far off a clock can be before a message is ignored.

sections.title: Registration Counters
sections.content:
The pmip6BindingRegCounters group holds read-only 32-bit counters. Many count Proxy Binding Update messages the LMA rejected, one counter per status code in the Binding Acknowledgement. Examples are 'Missing mobile node identifier option' (Code 160), 'Not authorized to send Proxy Binding Updates' (Code 154) and 'Not local mobility anchor for this mobile node' (Code 153). Other counters cover initial registrations, lifetime extensions, de-registrations and binding acknowledgements.

Counter discontinuities are flagged through pmip6CounterDiscontinuityTime.
sections.eli5: The panel keeps tally marks of how many requests were turned down and why, so a manager can spot a problem.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content: Four notifications are defined, two for the MAG and two for the LMA: pmip6MagHomeTunnelEstablished, pmip6MagHomeTunnelReleased, pmip6LmaHomeTunnelEstablished and pmip6LmaHomeTunnelReleased. They are sent every time the tunnel between the LMA and the MAG is established or released, and carry the tunnel interface identifier and the state of the proxy care-of address or LMA address.
sections.eli5: The panel rings a bell whenever the tunnel between the two helpers is opened or closed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Read-write objects can be sensitive. Setting pmip6MagStatus or pmip6LmaStatus enables or disables PMIPv6 on an entity, and misusing the timers or flags can disrupt communications. Some readable objects are sensitive too: the home network prefix objects and the mobile node identifier objects may identify users.

The RFC says SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementations MUST provide the SNMPv3 security features, including authentication and privacy through the User-based Security Model with the AES cipher. They MAY also support the Transport Security Model with SSH or TLS/DTLS. Operators remain responsible for giving access only to principals with legitimate rights.
sections.eli5: Because the panel can change how roaming works and shows who is connected, only trusted managers should be allowed to use it, and the messages should be locked.
